gvatua.name: Mikheil Gvatua
body: The academic year at the International Black Sea University opened with an award ceremony for distinguished professors.

At the event, the University honoured distinguished professors with more than 20 years of continuous academic work at IBSU, and the affiliated professors whose research was the most productive in the 2021–2022 academic year.
By decision of the University’s Governing Board, the title of Honorary Doctor was conferred on Mikheil Gvatua, an invited lecturer of the University.

strasse.name: Roman Strass
body: By decision of the Governing Board of the International Black Sea University of 14 May 2022, Roman Strass was awarded the title of Honorary Doctor.

The title was presented by the Rector of the University, who noted that Roman Strass is a longtime friend of the University, with a long and fruitful relationship with IBSU. “It is a great honour for the University Governing Board to award Mr Strass the title of Honorary Doctor,” the Rector said.

After the ceremony, Mr Strass thanked the Governing Board for the pleasant surprise and said that his active cooperation with IBSU would continue. He also spoke about the Eastern Partnership programme, Georgia–EU relations and European integration, and expressed his hope that the University’s students would contribute, as far as they can, to Georgia’s integration with Europe.

Mr Strass is a longtime friend and supporter of Georgia and its European future. He played a key role in forming the Group of Friends of Georgia in the European Parliament in October 2017 and became its first Secretary General. He has worked in European politics for more than 40 years.

mashkevich.name: Marius Mashkevich
body: The International Black Sea University held a ceremony to confer the title of Honorary Doctor of IBSU on Marius Mashkevich, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Poland.
In his address, the Ambassador spoke about Poland’s recent history, the Soviet legacy, and the political, economic and cultural relations between Poland and Georgia.

business.lede: The oldest school at IBSU — and the largest. Six undergraduate concentrations, three master tracks and a doctoral program in business administration, taught in Georgian and English by faculty who also consult, audit and build companies.
about: The School of Business prepares managers, analysts and entrepreneurs for an economy that is still, in many ways, being written. Programs pair a rigorous core in economics, accounting and quantitative method with concentrations that students choose from the second year.
Teaching is case-led and close to practice: students work on live company briefs, compete in international business games, and finish with a capstone consulting project for a real client.

life.body: Beyond the lecture hall, the school runs the activities where business is actually learned — clubs, competitions, and a steady stream of practitioners through the door.
list: Enactus & Investment Club — student ventures and a managed portfolio
CEO Talks — leaders from Georgian and regional firms
Startup incubator with the TEC center
Internships with banks, Big-Four firms & hotels

careers.body: Business is the most employable degree on campus. Graduates move quickly into banking, consulting, audit, marketing and their own ventures.

international.body: Business students are the most mobile at IBSU — a semester abroad is part of the plan, not an exception.
international.callout: Every concentration is offered in a fully English-taught stream, so an exchange semester abroad costs you no time toward your degree.

law.lede: Law and public governance under one roof. A Georgian-language LLB and a public-administration degree, taught by judges, prosecutors and practising advocates, with a moot court at the centre of the curriculum.
about: The School of Law trains lawyers and public servants for the courts, ministries and firms of a state still consolidating its institutions. The LLB combines Georgian private, public and criminal law with a strong comparative and EU-law component.
Skills are taught the way they are used: students draft, negotiate and litigate. The moot court, legal clinic and supervised internships in courts and law firms run throughout the degree.

life.body: The school is built around advocacy. Students argue, compete and represent — long before they graduate.
list: Legal clinic — free advice to the public

careers.body: Graduates enter the bar, the bench, the ministries and corporate legal departments — and the public-administration track feeds directly into the civil service.

stats.label: Pass the bar within two attempts

international.body: Law is taught in Georgian, but it is not taught in isolation — comparative and EU law, and exchange, keep the curriculum facing outward.
international.callout: Georgia’s EU-accession path makes EU law a living subject here — taught by faculty who advise on the harmonisation of Georgian legislation.

eduhum.lede: The widest-ranging school at IBSU, covering languages, international relations, media, psychology and education — and the only one offering programs at every level, from a first degree to a PhD and the teacher-training program.
about: This school holds the university’s humanist core: the study of language and culture, of how societies are governed and reported, and of how people learn. Several programs — American Studies, English Philology — are taught fully in English.
It is also the university’s teacher factory: the accredited teacher-training program and the master in educational administration prepare the people who will run Georgia’s classrooms and schools.

life.body: This is the most outward-facing school — a newsroom, a model-UN circuit, theatre, and a constant exchange of languages and cultures across the courtyard.

careers.body: Graduates teach, report, advise and represent — in schools, newsrooms, ministries, embassies and international organisations.

international.body: With English-taught degrees and US-focused programs, this school is where most of IBSU’s international students and partners converge.
international.callout: American Studies and US Foreign Affairs are anchored by an American Corner and a steady rotation of visiting US scholars — a genuine transatlantic window in Tbilisi.

journal.body: The school runs its own student publications: Vitascope, a peer-reviewed journal where undergraduates and graduates publish their first research, and its creative sister Dreamscape. Every issue is open to read online — and open to your byline.

computing.lede: Two ways of building the future under one roof: computer science and applied AI on one side, architecture and graphic design on the other. Graduate study runs entirely in English, and the school feeds directly into the TEC startup center.
about: The school combines a computing track — programming, systems, data and artificial intelligence — with a design-and-build track in architecture and, newly, graphic design. Studios and labs sit next to each other, and projects often cross between them.

Computing degrees are project-heavy and current: students ship working software, train models, and present at the school’s demo days. Architecture runs as a studio, with juries, models and site visits.

life.body: Building things together is the whole point — hackathons, studios, demo days and a direct line into the TEC startup center.

careers.body: Computing graduates are in the highest demand on campus — software, data and IT roles, at home and remote — while architecture and design graduates enter studios and practices.

international.callout: Because all graduate computing study is in English, the school’s master and PhD students publish, intern and exchange internationally without a language barrier.

medicine.lede: IBSU’s newest school exists for one purpose: a six-year, one-cycle Medical Doctor program, taught fully in English, leading directly to clinical practice. It is the university’s longest and most selective degree.
about: The MD program follows an integrated, systems-based curriculum: the pre-clinical sciences in the early years, clinical disciplines and supervised placements later, and a final clinical year in partner hospitals across Tbilisi.

It is designed to international standards so graduates can sit licensing examinations and practise beyond Georgia. The cohort is deliberately international, and the working language throughout is English.

life.body: Medicine is intense and communal — the cohort moves through six years together, supported by clinical skills labs, a student medical society and a genuinely international common room.

careers.body: The MD leads directly toward clinical practice. Graduates pursue licensing and residency in Georgia and abroad, supported by an internationally aligned curriculum.

international.body: This is IBSU’s most international school by design — an English-taught MD that draws students from across Asia, the Middle East and Europe.
international.callout: The MD program is built to international standards so that graduates can pursue licensing examinations and residency outside Georgia, not only within it.

studentMobility.title: Mobility
studentMobility.lede: Internal mobility between IBSU programmes and transfer from another university: who is eligible, matching the third exam subject and the master's test type, the documents you need, and frequently asked questions.

rights.heading: The right to mobility
body: IBSU students may use internal mobility (moving between IBSU's educational programmes) and mobility (transferring to another higher education institution) in line with the rules set by the legislation of Georgia.
Mobility is possible within one level of higher education.

Internal mobility is open to any IBSU student who has held active student status at IBSU for at least one semester, including students whose status is suspended at the time they register for internal mobility places.
The right to mobility arises after one year of study at the relevant level of higher education. Time during which the student's status was suspended does not count towards that year.
rights.matchLead: The right to mobility and internal mobility arises only for the programme direction that matches:
match: the type of general master's exam test the student passed — for master's students who sat the general master's exams before 2020;
the relevant third elective-compulsory subject passed at the Unified National Examinations — for students who passed them in 2020 or later.

rule.heading: The mobility rule set by the Minister's order
body: Under the order of the Minister of Education and Science of Georgia, the third compulsory subject passed at the Unified National Examinations must match the subjects required for the programme the student wishes to transfer to. Likewise, the type of general master's exam test (for students who sat the general master's exams before 2020) must match the test type required for the programme they are transferring to.

So, when writing a mobility application, the student must submit a document confirming that the subjects or test type they passed at the national exams or the master's exam match. If the match is not confirmed, the student cannot take part in mobility.

external.heading: External mobility
external.intro: Once you have confirmation of your transfer, send the International Black Sea University the following documents:
items: Application;
Copies of the documents that govern your student status (e.g. the act of enrolment, reinstatement, suspension or termination of status);
A transcript signed and stamped by an authorised person of your university, showing the credits and grade for each study component;

A document confirming that the subjects you passed at the national exams (if you passed the Unified National Examinations in 2020 or later) or your master's exam test type match the programme you are transferring to. If the match is not confirmed, you cannot take part in mobility;
A copy of your identity card (ID);
A certificate of complete general education and/or a copy of the document certifying completion of the previous level of higher education;
Two photographs (3×4), printed and in electronic form;
For male students: proof of military registration;

For enrolment at master's or doctoral level by mobility, if you present a diploma from a programme of at least five years completed within the period set by the Law of Georgia on Higher Education: a recognition document, issued as the law provides, confirming that the diploma is equivalent to the relevant level.
external.send: Send the application and documents to <mail>{email}</mail> with “Mobility” in the subject line, or hand them in at the University Chancellery. You are responsible for the accuracy of the documents you submit.

internal.intro: To use internal mobility, submit the following to the University's Records Management Office within the deadlines IBSU sets:
items: Application;

A document confirming that the subjects you passed at the national exams (if you passed the Unified National Examinations in 2020 or later) or your master's exam test type match the programme you are moving to. If the match is not confirmed, you cannot take part in mobility.

english.heading: From a Georgian- to an English-taught programme
english.intro: A student who uses mobility to move from a Georgian-taught to an English-taught programme must confirm the required level of English. The levels are:
levels: to enrol in the first semester of a bachelor's programme: at least the score in the English exam of the Unified National Examinations set for the receiving programme in that academic year (50%+1) or (60%+1);
to enrol in the second semester of a bachelor's programme: English at B1 level;
to enrol in the 3rd–5th semesters of a bachelor's programme: English at B2 level.
body: For master's and doctoral programmes, a student enrolling in a master's programme must confirm English at B2 level, and one enrolling in a doctoral programme at B2/C1 level, depending on the programme's admission requirements.

To confirm the required level, a student may submit an international English certificate; pass the English exam IBSU sets; submit a document showing they completed an English-taught study component at the same level whose learning outcomes reach B2/C1; or submit a document showing they completed an English-taught programme at the previous level within the last three years with a GPA of at least 75 (out of 100) or 3 (out of 4).

timeframe.q: When does external mobility take place at IBSU?
timeframe.a: The deadlines for external mobility are set by the Education Management Information System. They are published on its website, emis.ge, and on the International Black Sea University's website.

credits.q: What is the credit recognition procedure?
credits.a: To recognise the credits of a student who transfers by mobility, the Academic Process Management Service, together with the head of the relevant programme, prepares a comparison report and submits it to the Quality Assurance Service for review. The final version of the report is approved by the School Board. The student confirms in writing that they accept or decline the credits the University recognises; the Academic Process and Monitoring Service organises this.

outstanding.q: If I still have outstanding subjects at the university where I study, can I use mobility?
outstanding.a: Yes, you can. There is no restriction on this.

grants.q: Can I use internal grants during mobility?

foreignDiploma.q: What is the procedure if I hold a diploma issued abroad?
foreignDiploma.a: For a diploma issued in another country, you must submit a notarised translation recognised by the National Center for Educational Quality Enhancement.

foreignNationals.q: What are the terms for foreign nationals transferring to IBSU?
foreignNationals.a: Different tuition fees apply to foreign nationals. For details, write to the International Relations Office at iro@ibsu.edu.ge.

testWhen.q: When is the language placement test taken?
testWhen.a: If the documents a student submits do not establish the level of English the programme requires, the student must take a language placement test. It is held within the period for submitting mobility documents, and no later than the deadline by which IBSU's schools prepare their decisions and conclusions on credit recognition and on who is enrolled.

noTest.q: When is the test not needed?
noTest.a: When the required level is confirmed another way. A student can confirm it by: a) submitting an international English certificate; b) for first-semester bachelor's enrolment, having at least the English score at the Unified National Examinations set for the receiving programme in that academic year (50%+1), or (60%+1) for the English Philology programme; c) submitting a document showing they completed an English-taught study component at the same level whose learning outcomes reach the relevant B2/C1 level; d) submitting a document showing they completed an English-taught programme at the previous level within the last three years with a GPA of at least 75 (out of 100) or 3 (out of 4).

what.heading: What the Media Centre is
columns: The Media Centre of the journalism programme, Faculty of Social Sciences, International Black Sea University. Its purpose is to put what students learn in theory to work in practice.

The Media Centre is where the theory of the classroom meets the deadline of the desk. Students report real stories from campus and the city, film and edit them, present them on Radio IBSU and lay them out for the student newspaper — under the guidance of the lecturers who teach the programme.
Everything you read, watch or hear here was made by a student. It is a portfolio, a training ground and a public service all at once.

Seven desks cover the formats of modern journalism — daily news, on-the-ground reportage, long-form stories, interviews, photo reportage, multimedia and print. The campus radio and the student television make their own programmes. And every graduate leaves with a diploma film or thesis in the archive.
The Media Centre belongs to one school — Education, Humanities & Social Sciences — and carries its colour throughout.

scope.more: The journal welcomes original research articles, review articles and short communications. All submissions are evaluated for academic rigour, originality and relevance to the journal's scope.

editorial.intro: The editorial board brings together scholars from IBSU and partner universities across the region.

guidelines.intro: Manuscripts must be original, previously unpublished, and not under consideration elsewhere. Submissions are made through the journal's online system and undergo double-blind peer review. There is no submission or processing charge.

blocks.title: Language & length
blocks.body: Articles are accepted in English. Manuscripts should be 4,000–8,000 words including references, with an abstract of 150–250 words and 4–6 keywords.

blocks.title: Formatting
blocks.body: Times New Roman 12 pt, 1.5 line spacing, A4 with 2.5 cm margins. Tables and figures numbered consecutively. Use the APA 7th edition referencing style throughout.

blocks.title: Structure
blocks.body: Research articles follow: title, abstract, keywords, introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion, references. Author-identifying information must be removed to enable blind review.

review.intro: Every submission is screened by the editorial office and, if it fits the journal's scope, sent to at least two independent reviewers under a double-blind model — reviewers and authors remain anonymous to one another.

steps.title: Initial screening
steps.body: The editor checks scope, originality, structure and language. Out-of-scope or incomplete manuscripts are desk-rejected within two weeks.

steps.title: Double-blind review
steps.body: Two or more reviewers assess significance, methodology, and contribution, returning a recommendation: accept, minor revision, major revision, or reject.

steps.title: Decision & revision
steps.body: The editorial board makes the final decision based on reviewer reports. Authors revise and resubmit; revised papers may be sent for a second round.

steps.title: Publication
steps.body: Accepted articles are copy-edited, typeset and assigned a DOI before appearing in the next available issue under an open-access licence.

ethics.intro: The journal follows the principles of the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE). All parties — authors, editors and reviewers — are expected to uphold the highest standards of academic integrity.

about.heading: General introduction
body: The School of Law & Public Administration delivers quality education at bachelor's and master's level. Its academic and visiting staff are highly qualified professionals whose work combines teaching with a scholarly-research component. The school works closely with higher-education institutions and with the public and private sectors across every field of study — the best available means of building knowledge through empirical research. Alongside this, its students undertake practical work at partner institutions, both individually and under cooperation memoranda.

All of this lays the ground for accumulating knowledge and for future, ever-deeper research across every available direction. It is why we are building a law journal open to an unrestricted, diverse range of topics in the field.

focus.heading: Editorial focus
guidingBody: The development of Georgian law is a highly dynamic process that cannot be confined within narrow national frames. In line with the country's European orientation and the obligations of the Association Agreement, the domestic legal space must develop on a harmonised, unified legal basis — achieved first of all by studying European legislation, analysing practice, and adapting it to Georgian reality. Creating a scholarly forum that plays a meaningful part in this process is the aim of the journal.

The editorial board gives priority to studies of the existing legal system carried out by the comparative method. Due space is also reserved for work in the history and philosophy of law, alongside research produced together with other adjacent fields.
focus.circleBody: The circle of authors whose work appears in the journal is not restricted: submissions from experienced researchers and newcomers alike are welcome. Student participation in research — and the publication of its results — is especially encouraged, and we are equally open to research conducted with interdisciplinary methodology. IBSU students are supported to join the project “Study of Georgian Court Practice”, the results of which are published in a dedicated section of the journal.
focus.periodBody: The journal is published at least once a year. Depending on the volume of material submitted, we consider issuing special publications devoted to a particular sub-field or group of authors — the student forum in particular. Material for publication is edited by foreign specialists, and the editorial board — drawn from IBSU academic staff and other distinguished specialists — decides whether an article is published. The journal is bilingual, in Georgian and English, and available both in printed copies and online.

intro.heading: IBSU — where your path leads to the world's No. 1 university
body: The International Black Sea University (IBSU) and the world's leading institute of technology, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), are partners. The partnership gives our students and academic staff a unique opportunity to join the world's strongest entrepreneurial and innovation ecosystem. Through it, IBSU is a co-founder, alongside the world's leading universities, of the Global Leaders of the Entrepreneurship Educators Network (GLEEN), set up on the initiative of MIT's entrepreneurship centre, the Martin Trust Center for MIT Entrepreneurship. Hackathons, accelerators and pre-accelerators run regularly at IBSU in collaboration with MIT; the students who take part earn international certificates and gain real experience of working on entrepreneurial and innovation projects.

institute.heading: The institute we partner with
body: MIT is the undisputed leader of world innovation, and its model of entrepreneurship is recognised as the global standard. More than 30,000 active companies founded by its alumni (among them Intel, Moderna, Dropbox and AMD) create over 4.6 million jobs, and their combined annual revenue exceeds $2 trillion, the equivalent of the world's tenth-largest economy. The institute's venture fund, The Engine, is currently focused on "Tough Tech". This ecosystem shows that MIT is not just a school but a global economic engine that turns scientific discoveries into real, high-tech business empires.

quote: As a computer-science student, for me MIT is the place where technological ideas turn into business models.

StartMIT is a startup-acceleration program where experienced, professional speakers share their own experience and teach us how to develop a startup from idea to launch. Every topic was genuinely interesting — I'd especially single out choosing the target audience, Product-Market Fit and the pitching part.

MIT made a huge impression on me. The speakers were among the best and most successful figures in their fields, which made working with them especially valuable. I loved how direct they were — each shared their own experience, their failures, the road they travelled and the success they reached. Hearing their stories, in an open Q&A format, taught me how to avoid potential mistakes and be more consistent in building a startup.

ORBIT is a digital entrepreneurship platform built by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, focused on acquiring knowledge about technology startups quickly. It aims to structure the journey from forming an idea to going to market, to identify risks early, and to plan strategic steps.

inside.heading: What ORBIT gives IBSU
inside.lede: The platform brings together world-class knowledge and technological tools, available to a startup at any stage.

mission.heading: A competitive advantage
mission.body: IBSU's mission is to help develop a culture of entrepreneurship in Georgia. The MIT partnership and the ORBIT platform give IBSU's students and academic staff a unique competitive advantage — to build globally oriented businesses using international standards.

mitUniversalAi.title: Universal AI
mitUniversalAi.lede: Artificial intelligence for every IBSU student — MIT's programme on the foundations, the ethics and the practice of AI, with no prior coding and an international certificate at the end.

about.heading: What Universal AI is
body: Universal AI is the artificial-intelligence programme IBSU opens to its whole community through the MIT partnership. Every student and every member of the academic staff gets unlimited access — whatever school, whatever year, whatever background.

The programme starts from zero. It teaches what artificial intelligence actually is, how models are built and where they fail, the ethical questions they raise, and how to put AI to work in a real professional field — without asking you to write a line of code first.

faq.lede: Admission, tuition, grants, exchange and student life — the questions the offices are asked most.

intro.heading: Browse the answers
body: Can't find what you need? Reach the relevant office on one switchboard — +995 322 800 064 — or write to us from the contact page.

apply.q: How do I apply to a bachelor's programme?
apply.a: Georgian citizens are admitted through the Unified National Examinations. Put IBSU first on your list of choices, then submit your documents to the admissions office. International applicants apply through the International Relations Office.

language.q: Which programmes are taught in English?
language.a: IBSU is Georgia's first English-language university. Programmes are taught in English, Georgian, or both — the programme catalog lists the language of instruction for every one of them.

tuition.a: Annual tuition depends on the school and the level. The applicants page lists the full-price figures by school, and the grants calculator estimates what you would actually pay once grants are applied.

grants.a: IBSU runs several internal grants. Putting IBSU first on your list is what unlocks the internal grant.

exchange.q: Can I study abroad during my degree?
exchange.a: Yes — through Erasmus+, a bilateral agreement, or a seasonal school. You stay enrolled at IBSU and credits transfer back through a learning agreement.

accreditation.a: Every educational programme is accredited and the University itself is authorised. The programme catalog shows the date each programme's accreditation runs to.

emis.q: Where do I see my grades and schedule?
emis.a: In EMIS, the student information system. It holds registration, grades, your schedule, your financial account and official requests.

contact.q: How do I reach a specific office?
contact.a: Every office shares one switchboard — +995 322 800 064. Dial the extension once connected, or use the contact page to write to a team directly.
